title: Content with enough
hookLine: no disaster greater than not knowing what is enough (Tao Te Ching 46)

lines: WAR HORSES BRED ON THE BORDER.
cards: Two kinds of horses. In the first picture, the fast horses have been sent home to the farms, where they pull carts of manure out to the fields. Slow, dirty, useful work.
In the second, war horses are being bred out on the borders, foals born in army camps, far from any field.
Chapter forty-six of the Tao Te Ching sets these two scenes side by side, and says the difference between them comes down to one small thing.

teach.b: First, the horses. When the way is followed in the world, the chapter says, the swift horses go back to hauling dung for the fields. When the way is lost, war horses are bred on the frontier.
Peace looks humble: a racehorse pulling a farm cart. Trouble looks grand: armies at the edge of the map. Second, the cause.
There's no greater crime than giving in to desire, no greater disaster than not knowing what's enough, no greater fault than wanting to get more.
The war on the border starts long before the border, with a want that has no ceiling. Third, the turn.
In James Legge's translation, the chapter ends: "Therefore the sufficiency of contentment is an enduring and unchanging sufficiency." Say it slowly.
The enough that comes from contentment is an enough that lasts. Other kinds of enough keep moving: get the raise, and enough moves up with it. Fourth, the other side of a coin.
Earlier, chapter thirty-three said that whoever knows they have enough is rich. Chapter forty-six looks at what happens when nobody knows.
Bigger kitchens, fuller closets, longer lists, and the quiet war of always wanting the next thing. The chapter doesn't ask anyone to live with nothing.
It asks for one word said and meant: enough.
A full plate. A finished day. A home that holds the people in it.

how: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter forty-six as a reminder to name what is already enough, and some keep a habit of pausing before buying or adding more.

o: putting up with less than you deserve
having so little that you can't want more
knowing what's enough, an enough that lasts

p: swift horses haul dung for the fields
war horses bred on the frontier

s: chapter forty-six asks readers to live with nothing
it asks for knowing what is enough, not having nothing.
in the chapter, peace looks like racehorses pulling farm carts
when the way is followed, the swift horses go back to the fields.
the chapter says the enough of contentment keeps changing
in Legge's words, it is an enduring and unchanging sufficiency.

games.q: you get the raise you wanted, and a week later you want the next one. what does chapter forty-six point to?
o: aim higher; enough is for later.
the enough that comes from contentment.
games.why: the chapter says no disaster is greater than not knowing what's enough, and the sufficiency of contentment is the one that endures.

practice: Let your eyes or your mind rest on one thing in your life that is, right now, enough: the coat that keeps you warm, the breakfast you ate, a friend who calls, the breath in your lungs. Name it quietly: this is enough.
If you pray, you might give thanks for it; if you don't, just stay with it, and notice if the mind reaches for more.

wordCard.voice: Content with enough. Chapter forty-six: no disaster is greater than not knowing what's enough, and the enough of contentment lasts. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese: knowing what is enough, contentment; chapter forty-six says the enough of 知足 lasts.

carryVoice: Your line: enough is enough. Said and meant, it sends the horses home to the fields. Same time tomorrow.
